method: Live readBounded → articleExcerpt → prepareEvidence, one page at a time; S1 IDs are local to each pilot page, not future requests. Human-reviewed potential payoff, not generated posts.

sources.title: Theater in Ancient Greece
sources.proposedTitle: Why surviving theatres cannot settle the earliest Greek stage layout
sources.reviewedPayoff: Explains the evidence problem: repeated rebuilding obscures Classical spaces; the circular-orchestra evidence is dated, not a universal account of ancient seating.
sources.boundary: Do not turn absence of physical evidence into proof that no earlier circular orchestra existed.

support.text: Since theaters in antiquity were frequently modified and rebuilt, the surviving remains offer little clear evidence of the nature of the theatrical space available to
the Classical dramatists in the sixth and fifth centuries B.C.
There is no physical evidence for a circular orchestra earlier than that of the great theater at Epidauros dated to around 330 B.C.

sources.title: Greek Gods and Religious Practices
sources.proposedTitle: Athena’s armour did not exclude the workshop
sources.reviewedPayoff: A memorable cultural pairing: the armed goddess was also patroness of weaving and carpentry.
sources.boundary: Do not generalize one goddess’s attributes into a complete account of Greek religion.

support.text: Wise Athena, the patron goddess of Athens (1996.178), who typically appears in full armor with her aegis (a goatskin with a snaky fringe), helmet, and
spear (07.286.79), was also the patroness of weaving and carpentry.
The owl and the olive tree were sacred to her.

sources.title: Death, Burial, and the Afterlife in Ancient Greece
sources.proposedTitle: Achilles would rather serve the living than rule the dead
sources.reviewedPayoff: A specific episode from the Odyssey makes the bleak portrayal of the Underworld memorable.
sources.boundary: Identify this as Homeric myth and Achilles’ stated preference, not every Greek’s view of death.

support.text: It was not a happy place.
Indeed, the ghost of the great hero Achilles told Odysseus that he would rather be a poor serf on earth than lord of all the
dead in the Underworld (Odyssey 11: 489–91).

sources.title: Mystery Cults in the Greek and Roman World
sources.proposedTitle: What mystery cults offered beyond public ritual
sources.reviewedPayoff: Cultural context connects personal afterlife hopes, ritual reenactment and social bonds.
sources.boundary: Use the source’s “most” qualification for death-rebirth stories; the later numbered caveats warn against treating varied cults as one uniform religion.

support.text: A pendant to the official cults of the Greeks and Romans, mystery cults served more personal, individualistic attitudes toward death and the afterlife.
Most were based on sacred stories (hieroi logoi) that often involved the ritual reenactment of a death-rebirth myth of a particular divinity.
In addition to the promise of a better afterlife, mystery cults fostered social bonds among the participants, called mystai.

sources.title: TV's a crowd
sources.proposedTitle: Sympathy need not mean approval in The Sopranos
sources.reviewedPayoff: The critic acknowledges sympathy for repugnant protagonists while resisting the claim that television replaces cinema.
sources.boundary: Attribute this perspective to the critic; the offered opening does not supply the later visual-style argument or a plot example. Existing covered page: review only.

support.text: To an extent, I accept these claims: there’s little doubt that The Sopranos and Dexter break new ground in terms of audience identification, asking us
to sympathise unironically with protagonists whose behaviour and motivations we are simultaneously encouraged to find repugnant.
Yet I find myself unconvinced that American cinema is alive and well and available on HBO.

sources.title: The Paradox of Suspense
sources.proposedTitle: One account of suspense combines fear, hope and uncertainty
sources.reviewedPayoff: Explains the standard account with named attribution rather than promising to solve the whole paradox.
sources.boundary: The actual extraction starts at a substantive section; it does not supply a resolution of repeat-viewing suspense. Do not title the post as if it does.

support.text: Cognitive psychologists Ortony, Clore, and Collins put forth a useful theory of suspense that we might call the standard account.
On the standard account, people feel suspense when they fear a bad outcome, hope for a good outcome, and are uncertain about which outcome will
come to pass.

sources.title: Philosophy of Humor
sources.reviewedPayoff: A narrow historical detail distinguishes the newer use of the word from older discussion of laughter and comedy.
sources.boundary: This packet does not explain incongruity theory. Do not stretch the detail into a theory of why jokes work.

support.text: The word humor was not used in its current sense of funniness until the 18th century, we should note, and so traditional discussions were about
laughter or comedy.

sources.title: Fiction
sources.proposedTitle: Why factual departures are judged differently in fiction
sources.reviewedPayoff: The source contrasts standards of appraisal and uses historical novels as the concrete example.
sources.boundary: Do not infer that fiction has no ethical obligations or that all inaccuracies are harmless.

support.text: In whatever way we characterize the fiction/non-fiction distinction, the distinction is widely recognized as important. We care which category a work belongs to.
Historical novels such as Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1865–1867) or Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall (2009) also display bias and they depart in numerous ways from
fact, but the bias and inaccuracies don’t lessen their value as works of fiction.

sources.title: Public Goods
sources.proposedTitle: A grain of rice and a symphony explain non-rivalry
sources.reviewedPayoff: A concrete contrast explains why one person’s consumption can, or need not, diminish another’s.
sources.boundary: Do not conflate music with rival concert seats or claim this alone explains all public-goods policy; non-excludability is not in these selected IDs.

support.text: A good is rivalrous if and only if an individual’s consumption of it diminishes others’ ability to consume it.
Bob’s consumption of a grain of rice makes it impossible for Sally to consume the same grain of rice.
By contrast, Sally’s enjoyment of Bruckner’s Symphony No. 9 in no way diminishes Bob’s ability to do the same.

sources.title: The Ethics of Aristotle
sources.proposedTitle: Virtue as an active condition, not automatic routine
sources.reviewedPayoff: An attributed interpretive challenge turns on the translation of hexis and the difference between active character and passive habituation.
sources.boundary: Frame as this author’s reading rather than scholarly consensus. Existing covered page: review only.

support.text: These interpretations of Aristotle’s ethics are the result of imprecise translations from the ancient Greek text. Aristotle uses the word hexis to denote moral virtue.
But the word does not merely mean passive habituation. Rather, hexis is an active condition, a state in which something must actively hold itself.
Virtue, therefore, manifests itself in action.

sources.title: Roman Sarcophagi
sources.proposedTitle: A Roman coffin lid could look like a banquet couch
sources.reviewedPayoff: The kline lid gives a vivid cultural detail and identifies its Etruscan inspiration.
sources.boundary: Do not add a specific afterlife belief or imply that every Roman coffin had this form.

support.text: The most common shape for Roman sarcophagi is a low rectangular box (48.76.1) and a flat lid.
The kline lid, with full-length sculptural portraits of the deceased reclining as if at a banquet (1993.11.1), was inspired by earlier Etruscan funerary monuments.
This type of lid gained popularity in the later second century, and was produced in all three production centers for very lavish sarcophagi.

sources.title: Roman Copies of Greek Statues
sources.proposedTitle: Why a marble statue might need a tree trunk
sources.reviewedPayoff: A material mechanism: marble copies needed supports because they lacked bronze’s tensile strength.
sources.boundary: Keep the claim scoped to these marble copies; do not imply that every sculpted tree trunk is a support.

support.text: Artists used hollow plaster casts to produce bronze replicas. Solid plaster casts with numerous points of measurement were used for marble copies.
Since copies in marble lack the tensile strength of bronze, they required struts or supports, which were often carved in the form of tree trunks,
figures, or other kinds of images.

sources.title: The Many Saints of Newark and the baggage of The Sopranos
sources.proposedTitle: A prequel strongest when it steps away from its parent
sources.reviewedPayoff: A critic’s concise interpretive tension: the film’s strongest work is where it is furthest from the show.
sources.boundary: The three-ID cap cannot cover the longer social-history sentence plus this claim. Keep the post narrow; no extra plot or family details. Existing covered page: review only.

support.text: The weight of expectations doesn’t crush The Many Saints of Newark, but it’s at its strongest when far removed from The Sopranos, to which it
is a semi-prequel.
